clue.text: Facial expression when hastily. kissed, say

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: say signals that the following words are to be heard spoken, not read as spelt

parts.note: pecked means kissed quickly and lightly

explanation.surface: Someone's face changes as they are given a quick peck on the cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells you PECKED is to be heard, giving the sound PECT; AS (when) comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspect is the look or appearance on a person's face, an old literary sense of countenance.

clue.text: Served in the army — when disheartened, stuck together

indicators.note: disheartened means losing the heart, the central letter of the word

parts.note: soldiered means served as a soldier

explanation.surface: A veteran recalls army service, when morale was low but the unit held together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' removes the middle letter I from SOLDIERED.
explanation.definitionFit: To solder is to join metal with molten alloy, so soldered things are fastened together.

clue.text: Rulers showing false remorse about source of propaganda

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other
false means not genuine, so the letters are rearranged
source of means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Tyrants display fake regret for their propaganda campaigns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false' rearranges REMORSE into EMERORS, and 'about' puts it around P, the first letter of propaganda.
explanation.definitionFit: Emperors are sovereigns of empires, so they are rulers.

clue.text: Catchline, perhaps, relating to a particular craft

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A slogan seems to concern some specialist trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' shuffles the nine letters of CATCHLINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Technical means concerning the specialised skills of a particular art, trade or science.

clue.text: Attractive fine print

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads
an etching is a print taken from an etched plate

explanation.surface: Someone admires an attractive piece of small type in a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine print' reads as the small text of a contract, but it splits into F and a kind of print.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetching is a synonym for attractive or charming in appearance.

clue.text: Exploit flyer, with opponents on the retreat, and become richer

indicators.note: on in a down clue places one piece above the other

parts.note: a feat is a notable deed or exploit
a heron is a bird, a flyer
in bridge, East and South sit on opposing sides of the table
a nest is a cosy retreat or hideaway

explanation.surface: A daring airman, retreating with his rivals, ends up wealthier.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, East and South are opponents, giving ES; 'on' puts them above NEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To feather one's nest is an idiom for enriching oneself, often at others' expense.

clue.text: Talked about splendid chap, one stopping leaks

indicators.note: talked about means spoken, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a corker is British slang for an excellent person or thing

explanation.surface: People gossiped about a fine fellow who plugs leaks.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech CORKER and CAULKER sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A caulker seals seams in boats or windows to keep water out.

clue.text: One who brings in beer after motorway hold-up

indicators.note: after means this piece follows the one before it
in a down clue, held up means read upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written MI in crosswords
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A trader brings in beer after being delayed on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold-up' looks like a traffic jam, but in a down clue it lifts MI to read IM.
explanation.definitionFit: An importer brings goods into a country from abroad.

clue.text: A shy girl made up gaudily

indicators.note: made up means invented or put together, so the letters are assembled anew

explanation.surface: A bashful girl has put on make-up in a flashy way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made up' looks like make-up, but it shuffles the letters of A SHY GIRL.
explanation.definitionFit: Garishly means in a showy, lurid way, matching gaudily.

clue.text: Keep your hair on with this complaint? No!

definitions.text: Keep your hair on with this complaint? No!

parts.words: Keep your hair on with this complaint? No!
parts.note: keep your hair on is British slang for stay calm; the clue reads it literally, naming a medical condition in which the hair is lost

explanation.surface: Someone is told to calm down about their grumble, and refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep your hair on' is British slang for 'calm down', so 'complaint' looks like a grumble. Read literally, it asks what condition lets you keep your hair, and the answer is a condition that does the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Alopecia is the medical term for hair loss, a complaint that leaves you unable to keep your hair.

clue.text: Unusually large fender in US

definitions.meaning: a ... crop or harvest is an exceptionally big one
the protective bar on a car's front or back, which Americans also call a fender

explanation.surface: A remarkably big car fender is spotted in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumper is both an adjective for exceptionally big and the name of a car's protective bar.

clue.text: Tighten one's belt on kind of coat

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in business letters
a trench coat is a belted military-style raincoat

explanation.surface: A belt is pulled tighter around some sort of coat.
explanation.walkthrough: The belt seems to belong to the coat, since trench coats are belted, but 'Tighten one's belt' is the idiom for economising.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrench is to cut back spending, which is what tightening one's belt means figuratively.

clue.text: Bypasses used by Minis, for example

definitions.meaning: goes around the edge of something rather than through it
minis are short garments worn from the waist down

explanation.surface: Bypass roads are the routes Mini cars take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minis' suggests the British small car, which fits 'Bypasses' as roads, but here a mini is a short skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt is to go round the edge of something, and miniskirts are an example of the garment.

clue.text: Indent again, keeping carbon, for sound device

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to indent is to place an order for goods, so to indent again is to reorder
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: A typist sets an indent once more while keeping a carbon copy, all for an audio gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indent' suggests typing a set-in line, but in British commercial use it means to place an order.
explanation.definitionFit: A recorder is a machine for capturing sound, such as a tape recorder.

clue.text: Trace idea for cheating Excise.

indicators.note: cheating suggests something crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: Someone looks for a scheme to cheat the customs and duty office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excise' looks like the tax, but it is a verb meaning cut out; 'cheating' shuffles TRACE IDEA.
explanation.definitionFit: To excise is to cut out completely, which is to wipe out or remove.

clue.text: That's how we can specify this date this month

definitions.text: That's how we can specify this date this month

parts.words: That's how we can specify this date this month
parts.note: in the Roman calendar a fixed mid-month day was named, so one could say on that day of the current month

explanation.surface: Someone explains how to write down today's date for the current month.
explanation.walkthrough: The Romans counted dates from three named days; this one fell on the 13th or 15th, so 'this date this month' is a fixed mid-month marker.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ides were the Roman calendar's name for the middle day of each month.

clue.text: Press cards needed rigorous control

parts.note: to iron is to press clothes
a hand is the set of cards a player holds

explanation.surface: Journalists' credentials required strict supervision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press cards' reads as journalists' passes, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron hand is strict, harsh control, as in 'rule with an iron hand'.

clue.text: Specify old strong drink

parts.note: to express something is to state or specify it

explanation.surface: Someone names an old, potent liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a variant spelling of espresso, strong coffee; 'strong drink' suggests alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso, also spelt this way, is a strong concentrated coffee.

clue.text: Become strained in conflict

definitions.meaning: tempers or nerves become worn and tense

explanation.surface: Tempers become tense in the middle of a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: To fray is to become worn or strained, and a fray is a brawl or fight.

clue.text: Pretending an attack and collapsing when talking

indicators.note: when talking means the word is spoken, so its sound counts, not its spelling

parts.note: fainting means collapsing in a swoon

explanation.surface: A fighter fakes a blow and then keels over mid-conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: A feint is a sham attack, so feinting is making a pretended move to deceive an opponent.

clue.text: See scrappy game run over time, causing altercation

indicators.note: over in a down clue places the first piece above the second
scrappy means disorganised and ragged, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Watch a messy match run into extra time, provoking a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrappy' rearranges GAME RUN into ARGUMEN, which sits 'over' T in this down clue; 'See' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument is a heated dispute, the same as an altercation.

clue.text: Duck, elegant in motion, appearing to be slender

indicators.note: in motion means moving about, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: A graceful duck swimming along looks slim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in motion' shuffles O (a cricket duck, zero) with ELEGANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Elongate as an adjective means long and slender, chiefly in biology.

clue.text: Passes in English, overlooking ' 'slight errors

indicators.note: overlooking in a down clue means positioned above, so this piece comes first

parts.note: lapses are small slips or mistakes

explanation.surface: Someone lets small mistakes in English slide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' looks like ignoring, but in a down clue it puts E above LAPSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Time elapses when it passes by, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Country certainly not without king

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one piece is wrapped around the other

parts.note: no way is an emphatic refusal
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone flatly refuses to accept a nation that has no monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but here it carries its old sense of 'outside', so the refusal wraps around the king.
explanation.definitionFit: Norway is a Scandinavian nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Feudal lord who had the French right on his side

definitions.meaning: a lord of a manor under the feudal system

definitions.text: who had the French right on his side
definitions.meaning: the droit du ..., French for the lord's right, was a supposed feudal privilege

explanation.surface: A medieval landowner had French law in his favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the French right' is the droit du seigneur, the lord's supposed right over his vassals, so the phrase names its holder.
explanation.definitionFit: Seigneur is the French title for a feudal lord of a manor.

clue.text: Foolish fellows head of school had to judge

parts.note: asses are stupid people

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A headteacher was obliged to evaluate some silly men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of school' looks like a headteacher, but it just picks the first letter, S.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to evaluate or form a judgement about something.

clue.text: "Pass" is inappropriate if you can't give me an answer

definitions.text: "Pass" is inappropriate if you can't give me an answer

parts.words: "Pass" is inappropriate if you can't give me an answer
parts.note: the speaker is someone setting questions, for whom a candidate saying pass will not earn a pass mark

explanation.surface: A quizmaster warns a contestant that saying pass is no good if they cannot answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' is both what a stumped quiz contestant says and the grade an exam gives; the person who will not award it for no answer is the one marking.
explanation.definitionFit: An examiner sets and marks tests, deciding whether a candidate passes.

clue.text: Stroke entailing loss of point? Not necessarily

definitions.text: Stroke entailing loss of point? Not necessarily

parts.words: Stroke entailing loss of point? Not necessarily
parts.note: the words describe a gentle tennis or badminton shot whose name sounds like losing a point, though it often wins one

explanation.surface: A player wonders whether a certain shot will cost them a point.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'drop' plus 'shot', the name sounds like dropping a point; in fact this soft shot falling just over the net often wins the rally.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop shot is a soft stroke in racket sports that lands just beyond the net.

clue.text: Score less than a hundred

parts.note: a score is twenty, so take twenty away from one hundred

explanation.surface: A team's total falls short of a century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' looks like a match total, but it is the old word for twenty: a hundred minus a score.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighty is the number twenty short of one hundred, a score being twenty.
